sections.heading: What does COPD feel like, and how does it change over time?
sections.body:
The NHS says COPD develops slowly over many years, so people often do not notice it early on. The main symptoms it lists are breathlessness during activity, a long-lasting chesty cough with phlegm, frequent chest infections and wheezing. Phlegm is the thick mucus that is coughed up from the airways. COPD cannot be cured or reversed, and how it goes differs from one person to the next. For some people it gets worse despite treatment and can become life-threatening.

A flare-up, also called an exacerbation, is a time when symptoms become more intense than usual. An infection can make COPD worse, so a provider may prescribe antibiotics during a flare-up. A written action plan from the healthcare team can set out what to do when symptoms flare.

sections.heading: What are emphysema and chronic bronchitis, and who gets COPD?
sections.body:
COPD is an umbrella term for a group of lung conditions that cause breathing difficulties. Two conditions make up most of it. In chronic bronchitis, the airways stay inflamed and narrowed and produce mucus. In emphysema, the air sacs in the lungs are damaged over time. Most people with COPD have some mix of the two.

The NHS says COPD mainly affects older adults who smoke. It does not usually become noticeable until after the age of 35, and most people diagnosed are over 50. The CDC notes that smoking is the main cause, but people who have never smoked can also get COPD. The NHS also lists air pollution, workplace dust and fumes, and a rare inherited condition called alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency.

sections.heading: How is COPD diagnosed, and what happens at the appointment?
sections.body:
The NHS describes the process as starting with a conversation with a doctor about symptoms and smoking history. The doctor also examines the chest and may ask about weight and any family history of lung problems. A breathing test called spirometry is then usually arranged. It involves blowing into a machine, sometimes after a bronchodilator inhaler, which is a medicine that opens the airways. The readings are compared with normal results for someone of the same age, which can show whether the airways are obstructed. NICE advises suspecting COPD in people over 35 who have a smoking history and relevant symptoms, with spirometry supporting the diagnosis.

Other tests on the NHS pages include a chest X-ray, which helps rule out other lung problems such as chest infections or lung cancer. Blood tests can check for conditions with similar symptoms, such as anaemia, and sometimes for alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency. A CT scan or a phlegm sample may also be used.

sections.heading: What treatments are used for COPD, and what are they for?
sections.body:
The NHS says there is currently no cure, but treatment can help slow the condition and control symptoms. Options include stopping smoking, inhalers, pulmonary rehabilitation and, in rare cases, surgery or a lung transplant. NICE advises keeping the number and types of inhalers to a minimum, because fewer devices make them easier to use correctly. A GP may add a steroid inhaler if breathlessness continues or flare-ups are frequent. For a persistent chesty cough with thick phlegm, a doctor may suggest tablets that thin the mucus. Antibiotics may be prescribed for signs of a chest infection.

Pulmonary rehabilitation combines exercise and education, usually in group sessions. Long-term oxygen may be offered if the level of oxygen in the blood is low. Surgery is rare and includes bullectomy, lung volume reduction surgery and lung transplant.

sections.heading: How can people live well with COPD?
sections.body:
The NHS Devon page names stopping smoking as the most important step for a person with COPD who smokes. MedlinePlus suggests pursed-lip breathing, which helps save energy, slow the breathing and relax. Other self-care steps listed include taking long-term medicines every day, avoiding smokers and strong fumes, and doing breathing exercises.

Vaccination is recommended, and people with COPD are encouraged to have the yearly flu jab and the one-off pneumococcal vaccine. Living with COPD can also affect mental health, and anxiety and depression are more likely in people with long-term conditions including COPD. Starting treatment early matters, because the sooner it begins, the less chance there is of complications and flare-ups.

sections.heading: When should someone get medical help with COPD?
sections.body:
For a first suspicion, the NHS lists more breathlessness when exercising, a persistent cough with phlegm, frequent chest infections, wheezing, or a persistent chesty cough in a current or former smoker as reasons to see a GP. That is a routine GP appointment. For someone already diagnosed, MedlinePlus lists harder, faster or shallower breathing, fever, dark mucus, sleepiness, confusion or chest pain as reasons to contact the provider. In the UK this means NHS 111 or the GP the same day.

The NHS says to call 999 if very unwell with severe breathlessness, chest pain or coughing up blood. Complications can include cor pulmonale, which is swelling of the heart and heart failure caused by long-term lung disease.

faqs.a: The NHS says there is currently no cure for COPD, and the damage cannot be reversed. Treatment can help slow the condition and control the symptoms. The NHS lists stopping smoking, inhalers and pulmonary rehabilitation among the options. For many people, treatment can help keep COPD under control.

faqs.q: Is COPD the same as emphysema?
faqs.a: COPD is an umbrella term, and emphysema, where the air sacs are damaged over time, is one of its two main components. The other is chronic bronchitis, where the airways stay inflamed, narrowed and full of mucus. Most people with COPD have a mix of both.

No. The CDC says smoking is the main cause but people who have never smoked can also get COPD. The WHO names smoking and air pollution as the most common causes. The NHS also lists workplace dust and fumes and a rare inherited condition called alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency.

A flare-up, or exacerbation, is a time when COPD symptoms become more intense than usual. An infection can make COPD worse, which is why antibiotics are sometimes prescribed. A written action plan from the healthcare team helps people know what to do.

The NHS describes pulmonary rehabilitation as a programme that combines exercise and education. The NHS says programmes usually involve two or more group sessions a week for at least six weeks. MedlinePlus says it teaches exercises to improve breathing and the ability to exercise.

keyFacts.label: Type of condition
keyFacts.value: COPD is a group of long-term lung conditions that cause breathing difficulties.

keyFacts.label: Main symptoms
keyFacts.value: Breathlessness on activity, a long-lasting chesty cough with phlegm, frequent chest infections and wheezing.

keyFacts.label: Who it mainly affects
keyFacts.value: Older adults who smoke; it does not usually become noticeable until after the age of 35.

keyFacts.label: Main test
keyFacts.value: A breathing test called spirometry, alongside questions about symptoms and smoking and a chest examination.

keyFacts.label: Cure
keyFacts.value: No cure currently, but treatment can help slow it and control symptoms.

keyFacts.label: Common treatments
keyFacts.value: Stopping smoking, inhalers, pulmonary rehabilitation and, if blood oxygen is low, long-term oxygen.

keyFacts.label: Vaccines
keyFacts.value: Yearly flu jab and a one-off pneumococcal vaccine are encouraged.
